We use the procedure on TD-MPC2 (decoder-free world model) that has learned the pendulum swing on an observation lift under varying hyperparameters at k = 5, 10, 25 steps. The model is then steered within a PCA-derived intervention subspace and compared against a ground-truth simulator using relative error to investigate dynamical faithfulness. ARC sufficiency held for TD-MPC2 most consistently at k = 10, with six of seven constraints statistically significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction, while the relative error between the simulator and the causal latent remained substantial. Further research could be conducted with decoder world models such as DreamerV3 (reconstruction loss) to investigate whether the results differ.

items.title: LEAP-LLM: Preserving lead-time structure for question-conditioned ECG interpretation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18809v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The electrocardiogram (ECG) records cardiac electrical activity across multiple leads and is used for detecting cardiac abnormalities. Recent ECG-language models enable large language models (LLMs) to interpret cardiac signals and answer clinically relevant questions. However, existing ECG-language models typically encode the ECG independently of the clinical question, forcing the ECG representation to retain broad and potentially irrelevant signal information. Moreover, these models often aggregate information across leads which can obscure lead-specific details needed for a particular question. To tackle these limitations, we introduce LEAP-LLM, an ECG-LLM architecture for Lead-aware ECG Alignment with Prompt conditioning. LEAP-LLM uses the clinical question to guide ECG feature extraction while preserving explicit lead and temporal structure. Task-trained instruction representations distill information from the question and guide two complementary branches. The Lead branch captures question-relevant temporal patterns within each ECG lead, while the Temporal branch summarizes relevant information across leads at each temporal position. Together, they provide the LLM with compact, question-relevant ECG information while preserving lead and temporal structure. LEAP-LLM reduces modality-token count by 89.0% and prefill FLOPs by 7.2x on average relative to other ECG-LLMs baselines. Across four ECG benchmarks, LEAP-LLM achieves better performance, including a 3.4-percentage-point improvement in G12EC over the strongest prior ECG-specific method. We further show that the model adaptively emphasizes the clinically relevant anatomical lead groups for different cardiac abnormalities, with lead importance patterns consistent with established diagnostic knowledge, providing interpretable evidence that the predictions are supported by clinically meaningful ECG structure.

items.title: What to Practice Next? Latent Profile-Guided Task Selection for Skill-Evolving LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18818v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Task selection shapes the experiences available for skill evolution in LLM agents, yet fixed practice schedules overlook differences in skill requirements and evolving task value. Most existing methods, however, rely on fixed schedules or scalar measures of progress, leaving nonstationary skill demands unaddressed. We propose SPG-Select, a framework for allocating limited practice budget using a multidimensional profile inferred from binary outcomes via MIRT. The framework predicts surrogate progress, defined as the difference between consecutive profile estimates, and prioritizes progress in dimensions with larger estimated proficiency gaps. Our SPG-Select-R policy combines these predictions with uncertainty-based exploration and periodic restarting to accommodate nonstationarity. We evaluate SPG-Select on ALFWorld and WebShop with three skill-evolution backends. In the reported runs, SPG-Select-R achieves higher mean held-out terminal success than uniform sampling in all six backend-benchmark combinations, with gains of 1.49-13.18 percentage points on ALFWorld and 0.93-3.13 points on WebShop. Under a predictable linear surrogate model and boundedness assumptions, we establish a high-probability dynamic pseudo-regret bound for surrogate task allocation in terms of parameter path variation.

items.title: Identification and external validation of the sets of 4-, 6-, 8-, 12-, and 24-hour CGM motifs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: There is growing interest in using CGM for purposes other than those initially intended. Recent work of Lobo et al. identified $\Omega$: a set of motifs such that almost any daily CGM profile (the 24-hour CGM time series starting at midnight) can be classified - matched to a motif in $\Omega$. This work generalizes the prior work by identifying sets of motifs for 4-, 6-, 8-, 12-, and 24-hr CGM profiles where an $x$-hr CGM profile does not have to be 24 hours in length, and does not have to start at midnight. The prior work methods are modified to identify the five new sets of motifs using data from the same 6 studies in the original work. The newly identified sets were subjected to rigorous external validation using a data set comprised of data from 21 studies (3,455 subjects, 289,592 days of CGM data). The external validation data set has both temporal and geographic transportability and addresses limitations of the data set used to define the five new sets of motifs. The results of the external validation indicate that the prior work generalizes well: the performance of each $x$-hr set of motifs on the external validation set is almost identical to that obtained for $\Omega$. The generalization of the original work broadens the potential use cases of the framework to include short term predictions (e.g., impending hypoglycemia) and diagnostics which rely on detecting changes in CGM time series which are less than 24 hours in length.

items.title: Self-Improvement Memory Enables Continual Recursive Self-Improvement
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18856v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Harness optimization is often studied with a fixed policy model and benchmark. When either changes, the optimizer must decide which parts of an evolved harness to reuse or revise, but the harness alone may not explain why earlier edits were made or how they performed. In this work, we study Continual Recursive Self-Improvement (CRSI), a setting for continuing existing harness-optimization methods across compatible benchmarks or policy models. We propose Self-Improvement Memory (SIM) for the harness optimizer, rather than the task-solving policy. SIM groups edits by recurring harness problem and records their rationale, predicted and observed outcomes, and evaluation context. New attempts extend this history as optimization continues. In our experiments across four domains, SIM achieves higher final scores than harness-only and root-cause-only continuation in cross-dataset and pairwise cross-model comparisons. Across ten independent source runs in coding, paired continuations with SIM improve final scores by an average of 2.36 points over harness-only continuation ($p=0.003$).

items.title: SLICES: A Benchmark and Evaluation Framework for Self-Supervised Learning on Sparse ICU Time Series
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18868v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) results for intensive care unit (ICU) time series are hard to compare when data processing, encoders, and adaptation vary together. We present SLICES, a benchmark and evaluation framework for comparing and extending SSL methods under a shared clinical setup. It fixes 24-hour value and observation-mask inputs, a Transformer encoder, patient-level splits, four endpoints, two adaptation protocols, and five matched seeds across MIMIC-IV, eICU-CRD, and their pooled union. Masked autoencoding (MAE), joint-embedding prediction (JEPA), and contrastive learning provide reference implementations. Among these objectives, MAE leads mean AUPRC in all nine frozen classification comparisons, also under converged probes, and in seven of nine fine-tuning comparisons. Fine-tuned MAE leads hospital mortality at full labels and scores higher than a supervised Transformer of the same architecture at every label fraction, and SSL fine-tuning gives the lowest length-of-stay error. Supervised baselines remain strong elsewhere: GRU-D leads 24-hour mortality and XGBoost leads acute kidney injury in all three regimes. Rankings depend on the adaptation protocol, the comparator set, and whether the probe loss matches the metric. A two-seed MIMIC-IV rerun with the maintained code stays within two across-seed SDs of the reference in all 48 downstream runs. The code repository supports new objectives, shared downstream evaluation, and regeneration of the reference results, so new SSL methods can be compared with these references under the same conditions. Generalization to unseen hospitals is not tested here and is the natural next extension.

items.title: Factorized Self-Supervised Speech Tokenization
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18898v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speech tokenizers convert audio into discrete units, enabling language models to process and generate speech. The goal is to learn compact, text-like representations while preserving enough detail to reconstruct a speaker's voice and delivery. We propose Facto: a factorized tokenizer that disentangles time-varying information (content and prosody) from static components (speaker identity and recording conditions). We build on a recent linear factorization method for self-supervised features, extending it to handle unseen speakers. Then, we cluster the factorized space and train a lightweight decoder to reconstruct audio from the resulting tokens. By removing the static components before clustering, our tokens are more robust to small noise perturbations. We validate this by testing token stability under various noise conditions. Next, we theoretically analyze Facto's convergence and scaling properties, quantifying how the factorization improves with the number of training speakers. Finally, we evaluate Facto on a range of downstream tasks. We show that greater token stability translates into improved text-to-speech performance and competitive results in voice conversion and spoken language modeling. Code and checkpoints at https://github.com/ubisoft/ubisoft-laforge-facto/ and demo page at https://ubisoft-laforge.github.io/speech/facto/.

items.title: How Much Do Foundation Models Add to Gradient Boosting on Financial Event Sequences?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18914v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Foundation models pretrained on raw transaction sequences are proposed for credit, fraud and churn modeling, with reported gains over gradient boosting, but the data and baselines behind these gains are rarely public. We measure how much the pretraining and adaptation recipes of these models add to a baseline of point-in-time window aggregates and LightGBM, and we propose TBS (Temporal Boosting-Sequence ensemble), which averages the ranks of a boosting model enriched with label-free event-transition features and of a pretrained sequence network fine-tuned jointly with the aggregates. On a synthetic credit-card dataset, the public MBD-mini banking dataset and two proprietary datasets of trade credit and B2B churn, we compare 27 methods at three label budgets with five seeds and paired bootstrap intervals, using sequence models of about 0.4 million parameters pretrained per dataset. Frozen self-supervised embeddings rarely improve the baseline, and a fine-tuned sequence network alone clears it in 9 of 21 target-budget cells. TBS clears it in 19 of 21 cells (18 after FDR adjustment), with a median gain of +1.8 AUC points, and the controls suggest that combining boosting with the pretrained network is the main source of the observed gain. Gains shrink as labels grow and with rich tabular data: with both, the gain on the proprietary datasets is +0.7 and +0.8 points, the latter with an interval including zero. We also re-examine two benchmarks. On IBM TabFormer, the test follows a change in the fraud pattern and the published baseline has no history; with the training period the vendor states, our history-aware LightGBM and our own foundation model stay below the published scores of a commercial model. On IBM AML, a simulation artifact lets a date rule reach F1 0.482, and a point-in-time LightGBM reaches the F1 of graph neural networks whose test graph includes later transactions.

items.title: The Human Side of ML Engineering: Analyzing the Collaboration and Communication Skills in ML Job Postings
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18915v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Studies of Machine Learning (ML) practice highlight the importance of combining technical expertise with interpersonal capabilities, particularly collaboration and communication. However, evidence on how ML job postings express these skills is scarce, and prior work largely relies on keyword-based analyses that overlook implicit expression. We analyze demand for these skills in ML job postings across regions, industries, and seniority levels, and compare it with software engineering (SE) roles. We collected 1,000 postings (500 ML, 500 SE) from five continents via a semi-automated pipeline. For annotation, we synthesized a taxonomy of collaboration and communication sub-categories from prior work and used an LLM as a third annotator alongside two humans, enabling detection of context-dependent and implicit skill references. Collaboration appeared in 88.6% of ML postings and communication in 72.2%, far above prior keyword-based estimates for AI roles. Roughly one in five collaboration and one in four communication requirements were expressed only implicitly. Decomposing these requirements into the taxonomy's sub-categories reveals what aggregate figures conceal. Collaboration is demanded predominantly as integration across role boundaries rather than team membership. Communication is mostly required in generic terms, with fewer than half of the postings requiring it naming whom the candidate must communicate with. ML and SE postings demand interpersonal competence at statistically indistinguishable levels but orient it differently, SE toward team practices and ML toward presentation and audience-facing interaction. Within ML, the advertised role separates interpersonal profiles more sharply than any other dimension, including the contrast with SE.

items.title: Simplify, Agree, Distill: Label-Free Self-Distillation with Stepping Stones
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18916v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can a language model teach itself to reason without labels? On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses the model as its own teacher, but strengthens that teacher with a ground-truth solution. The natural label-free substitute, voting over the model's attempts, fails precisely on hard problems: attempts disagree, and their most common answer is often wrong. We propose STONE, a label-free alternative that moves agreement to easier related problems. The model writes these stepping stones, keeps those it solves consistently, and shows the teacher their worked solutions, with final answers removed; the student sees only the original problem. No step reads a label, and inference needs no extra context or model calls. Across five math benchmarks, the proposed method achieves the highest average accuracy for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B in thinking mode. Without thinking mode, it gains 13.2 and 22.7 points, 2.5 and 2.7 times the gains of OPSD with ground-truth solutions.

items.title: Show HN: TrnRT – An open-source LLM inference engine for AWS Trainium
items.summary: Hi HN, Sanchit here from RunAnywhere (YC W26). We just open-sourced TrnRT: Trainium RunTime, our inference engine for AWS Trainium. We started 3 weeks back, and currently we’re able to serve and run GLM 5.3 flash (FP8) on AWS trn2.48xlarge, and will bring more models support soon. It’s open to contributions :) What it does today: - Serves 2 instances of GLM-5.3 flash on a single box, 8 trn2 with a cache aware router. - Can process 3.57M TPM (tokens per minute) on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks. - Runs decode as one NKI kernel per layer half, or for the 11 sparse-attention layers fuses both blocks into a single kernel, for faster performance. We started working on Trn2 because we wanted to explore it and see if we can come close to beating it’s performance in terms of cost efficiency compared to H100/H200. A big MoE with 1M context window such as GLM-5.3 flash requires a lot of memory, and memory/tb on a trn2.48xlarge costs less than half compared to 8x h200 on AWS, and hence we wanted to experiment with it and now we’re sharing some early results. But AWS's own stack didn't support the model: vLLM Neuron's latest release did not register any GLM model, and NxDI, AWS's own distributed inference framework, is no longer under active development. We also saw the drop of SGLang Neuron implementation yesterday, but there is no good support for Trn2, which is the only chip available for public use right now. We ran semiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks, which replays real coding agent sessions: - 1 box served 28.9 RPM(requests per minute) with 32 agents at batch 12 (also known as concurrency) -The P50 TTFT with a cached prompt at 16 agents is ~1.24 seconds with a decode of 35.9 tps. Initially, the recurrence in one kda (linear attention) layer was ~2% of the layer's attention time at batch 1, and the rest was projections, transposes and XLA glue between small kernels. So we wrote the megakernel so that it covers the whole layer in 2 kernel dispatch, which made decode 25% faster at batch 8. The sparse attention kernel keep a layer’s working weights in SBUF, distributing weighted streaming across the cores and handling the interchip communication within There’s an approximation in the sparse-attention prefill, affecting about 1.2% of block selections. You can refer to the write-up for the profiling results: https://runanywhere.ai/blog/glm-5-3-flash-trainium2-nki-mega... Please give it a try yourself on a trn2.48xlarge and reproduce the AgentX results by following the steps in docs/RESULTS.md. Happy to collaborate and hear any feedback. Deploying high performant dedicated inference at lab like performance and half the price for open models such as the GLM-5.3 family, Kimi K3, Deepseek flash etc. is how we make money. You can talk to us regarding the same at founders@runanywhere.ai. We hope you find this useful. If you are working with Trainium or have experience with NKI kernels, we'd love to get your honest feedback. Feel free to share the models you want support for next, and we welcome any contributions to the repository. Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50533270 Points: 13 # Comments: 1

items.title: Show HN: Zigzag, a native Mac browser for people leaving Arc
items.summary: Hello HN! I am Zigao, a high school student from Shanghai. I am new to HN so hello to y’all! I used Arc everyday, and I never had any issues with it. So when The Browser Company announced that they will shut down Arc on Dec 22 I was devastated. I don’t want to switch back to boring tabs along the top. Everything else i’ve tried is either a Chromium fork or an AI integrated browser that I don’t want. Therefore, I’ve been building my own browser for the last three weeks. Its name is Zigzag, a free and open source Mac browser that works just like Arc, written in Swift and based on WebKit. It is lightweight and fast. Zigzag has: - The stuff you missed from Arc (obviously, that’s the point)... - Import from Arc (or any other browser) brings everything (your spaces, pins, history, passwords, cookies, etc) - Chrome extension support! Even though its based on WebKit, you can install them from the Chrome Web Store. Extensions such as 1Password, Bitwarden, dark reader, Return Youtube Dislike, Tampermonkey all work) And most importantly: - Privacy: no account, no telemetry, no analytics - Free and open source: no one can shut it down, anyone can contribute and fork their own copy! - It’s tiny and fast! Around 18 MB installed (Arc is over 800 MB), no Chromium, no Electron (eww) Some minor features that are nice-to-haves: - Built in ad blocker using uBlock origin’s and Easylist’s filter lists - Cookie popups turned down for you automatically, never accepted - Split view up to four pages, drag pages intuitively - Install any website as apps (still polishing it) - Developer mode for web devs - Little Arc (called Zigzag Mini) - AI apps can use your browser if you want (MCP, off by default), stop button built in - AppleScript and Shortcuts support, written in the conventional way Why WebKit? - I once tried to fork Helium and build on that. But the source was around 100 GB and builds took 3 to 4 hours on my Mac. Shipping Chromium is nearly impossible for me as a solo dev - Battery and RAM: WebKit is built for Mac by Apple, its generally easier on battery and memory than Chromium - Native: Swift + WebKit = behaves like a real Mac app, explained later (e.g. Zen) - Chrome extensions already works on Zigzag, so the point of using Chromium is mostly gone Why not Zen or Orion? I tried both before building this, because I was looking for alternatives. They are good browsers, just not what I wanted. Zen is based on Firefox. It is basically an Arc replica but it’s a Firefox under the hood, so you get Firefox extensions instead of Chrome extensions, and it doesn’t really feel like a native Mac app, which was kinda backwards. If you love Firefox it’s great, but it didn’t feel like Arc to me. Orion is the closest to what I wanted in terms of speed, lightweightness and nativeness (are these even words?). It is WebKit and runs Chrome extensions. But it is closed sourced, and it is nowhere like Arc. It has vertical tabs but no real spaces, pins or favorites like Arc. It feels like a Safari clone instead of an Arc clone, so I turned it down. I love how it supports Chrome extensions, so that’s why I’ve done the same in Zigzag. So how do Chrome extensions work on WebKit? This is probably the part people ask about the most, so here you go. In macOS 15.4, Apple added web extension support to WebKit itself. Safari only takes extensions that come wrapped in an app from the App store, but the engine underneath can load a normal Chrome extension folder. So when you click “Add to Zigzag” on the Chrome Web Store, Zigzag downloads the extension straight from Google. It checks its signatures, unpacks it, and hands it to WebKit. That’s the easy part, and frankly most WebKit browsers can do that easily. However, WebKit doesn’t have every Chrome API. Stuffy like history, bookmarks, downloads, side panels, notifications and a few others just aren’t there. So Zigzag fills those in itself. When an extension calls one, Zigzag answers it, but only if that extension asked for that permission. 1Password and Bitwarden works, because they talk to their Mac apps the same way they do in Chrome. The hardest one was Tampermonkey. WebKit has no userScripts API at all, so I had to build my own on top of WebKit’s content scripts, with each extension’s scripts kept separate from the extension itself like in Chrome. What doesn’t work yet: - the debugger API (so things that control the browser like Claude for Chrome cant control the pages, but there’s MCP that you can turn on if you want) - Chrome’s own Google sign in for extensions (chrome.identity) - Some old way of blocking requests that some extensions still use (webRequest from manifest V2) (e.g. uBlock origin full doesn’t work, but lite version works) Most popular extensions are fine though. If any extension doesn’t work, leave a comment below or open an issue and I will look into it. How I build it Honest up front: I built Zigzag with the help from Claude Code. But it is not another piece of AI slop app. I decide what it does and how it should feel, and every change goes through my own daily browsing before it ships. It is my daily browser now for three weeks, and I am just like any of you, I don’t want trash apps! Claude writes most of the code, but I am the one reviewing the quality, the functions and the UI/UX decisions. Try it out yourself or open a PR if you can do better! What’s missing It is still a beta. No sync between Macs yet (passwords sync through iCloud keychain though). No boosts or easels. Needs macOS 15.4 or newer. Try it https://zigzagbrowser.com https://github.com/ZigaoWang/zigzag If you try it I’d love to know what didn’t went so well (or what did went well!), which extensions you need, and any sites that break. I read every issue on GitHub and every comment below! Thank you for your time! Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50496787 Points: 99 # Comments: 61
